title: Rain, Dew and Weather
lead: The promised land "drinks water from the rain of the sky" (Deuteronomy 11:11), so the Bible watches the weather closely: the early and late rains, dew, wind, thunder, snow and hail, all sent by God. Drought and hunger have their own page (Famine).

sections.h: A land that waits for rain
sections.b:
In Egypt a farmer "watered it with your foot, like a vegetable garden," but the promised land "is a land of hills and valleys" that depends on rain from God (Deuteronomy 11:10–12). He promises "its rain at the right time, the early rain and the late rain" (Deuteronomy 11:14). The Hebrew words are yoreh (also moreh), the autumn rain, and malqosh, the spring rain; Jeremiah speaks of God "who gives rain, the autumn and the spring rain, / each at its time" (Jeremiah 5:24; compare Joel 2:23; Hosea 6:3; Zechariah 10:1). James borrows the picture: the farmer waits "until it receives the early and the late rains" (James 5:7). Dew mattered too, as a blessing (Genesis 27:28; Hosea 14:5) and a sign for Gideon (Judges 6:37–40). Samuel called down thunder and rain at the wheat harvest as a sign (1 Samuel 12:17–18). After the flood God promises that "seedtime and harvest, cold and heat" will not stop (Genesis 8:22), and sets his bow in the clouds (Genesis 9:13).

Jewish prayer still follows this year. The Mishnah teaches that Jews begin to mention "the might of the rains" at the feast of Sukkot in the autumn and ask for rain from early in the month of Marheshvan until about Passover (Mishnah Taanit 1:1–3).

sections.h: Rain from the LORD, not from Baal
sections.b:
The Canaanites credited rain to Baal, and Elijah's challenge is about who sends it: "these coming years will have no dew and no rain unless I give the word" (1 Kings 17:1), until "a little cloud, like a person's hand" rises from the sea (1 Kings 18:44; compare James 5:17–18). Jeremiah asks, "Can any of the nations' empty idols make it rain?" (Jeremiah 14:22). Thunder is "The LORD's voice" (Psalm 29:3–9; Job 37:2–5); he "lets the wind out of his storerooms" (Psalm 135:7) and asks Job, "Have you walked into the places where snow is stored?" (Job 38:22; compare Psalm 147:16–18). Hail falls on Egypt (Exodus 9:23–24) and on the armies fleeing down the slope of Beth-horon (Joshua 10:11). The hot east wind withers grain (Genesis 41:6), drives back the sea (Exodus 14:21) and strikes Jonah (Jonah 4:8). Jesus stills the wind with a word (Mark 4:39), and he teaches that the Father "sends rain on righteous and unrighteous people" alike (Matthew 5:45; compare Acts 14:17).

Jesus also expects people to read the sky: a cloud from the west means rain and a south wind means heat (Luke 12:54–55), and a red sky at evening means good weather (Matthew 16:2–3). His complaint is that they read the weather but not the time they are living in.

sections.b: Several verses describe water going round: "All the streams go to the sea, / and still the sea is not full" (Ecclesiastes 1:7); God "pulls up the water drop by drop; / they filter into rain from his mist" (Job 36:27); he "summons the sea's waters / and pours them out over the face of the earth" (Amos 9:6; Amos 5:8); he "lifts the clouds from the edge of the earth" (Psalm 135:7). These verses fit the cycle of evaporation and rain that science later described in detail; whether the writers meant a theory, or simply put into words what anyone could see, the sea feeding the clouds, the text does not say. Older readers had other explanations: Rashi taught that the rivers' water flows back to its sources through channels under the mountains. The Greek of Job 36:27 reads differently, saying the drops of rain are numbered by God. On every reading the Bible's point is that the whole round of water is in God's hands.
